posts.name: Sayan Ghosh
posts.cooked:
@all please engage in constructive and well-formed discourse instead of banter. This is not a chat forum. Please take time to form your thoughts, lay them out properly, and only reply if you have something helpful or positive to contribute.

@23f2003845 is correct, the $$ gives the process id (or PID) of the current shell, which is then passed to grep, thus grep is told to match lines that have that process id. Obviously process id is unique, and hence only one line matches, that of the parent bash shell.

It will obviously not be same for you and the question, PIDs are allocated everytime a process runs and depends on processes running in the system. The point of this question is to

  • know what $$ does → it returns PID of the shell in which it is running
  • know that bash is the shell we are running
  • understand that bash processes variables before passing it to the grep command as argument.
  • No, $$ and "$$" have no difference, they are equivalent
  • After bash converting $$ to 64754 in the question, or 39690 in your case, it is given to grep and grep tries to find that number in the output of ps, which is present only in the line of bash
  • That is then printed.
